comments.author: mturmon
comments.why: DeepMind demo learning games from only the video signal
comments.text: Thanks for the correction. The "arbitrary" qualifier is not in TFA, but (as, indeed, you said) that's the point of the demo, e.g.: [VIDEO] Note that they're using just the video signal from the game as input. It's really a sad comment on the state of reporting at MIT Tech Review that you learn more about the tech from a youtube video than from an article. (My complaint is not with the DeepMind people, it's with the article, which should put the work in context.)

comments.author: paulsutter
comments.story: Why 2015 Was a Breakthrough Year in Artificial Intelligence
comments.why: DeepMind Atari player uses score as reward
comments.text: AGI is the idea of creating general intelligence. Which almost certainly requires some reinforcement learning (the ways dogs and humans learn, by having a goal and an internal reward system). Deepmind's Atari player is based on deep reinforcement learning, where increasing the score represents a reward: [VIDEO] I used to believe the moving goalpost idea, that AI is anything that isn't yet possible. I now disagree. I saved myself a lot of energy by avoiding entirely the question "what counts as AI?" by switching to the question, "what counts as AGI?" which is a term with a clearer threshold: [LINK]

comments.author: paulsutter
comments.story: Deep Learning – Review by LeCun, Bengio, and Hinton
comments.why: Example of impressive deep reinforcement learning progress
comments.text: I was also under the misapprehension that deep learning is just about classification, but that isn't true. Yes, reinforcement learning is the path to general intelligence, and the deep learning community is showing impressive progress on that front as well. The Deepmind demo [1] and the recent robotics work at Berkeley[2] are good examples. Thanks for the link to Stan Franklin's work. I'm glad to hear there is work to integrate the two approaches.
